title: Zonal eviction thresholds — playback + quick debug notes
content:
Quick context:
We saw a customer-facing surge yesterday that triggered a multizone eviction cascade for a small subset of hosted API routes. This doc is my scratch playback of what I did, commands run, and hypotheses that still feel plausible. Intention: capture commands/outputs so others can reproduce locally and to avoid repeating dumb checks.

High-level observed behaviour:
- Time window: 2026-03-08 17:42–18:05 UTC.
- A traffic spike (short, high-QPS) to route /v1/generate led to uneven capacity scoring across AZs. AZ-east-2 dropped below the eviction threshold and started ejecting pods/encaps, which caused a transient global routing re-election and then further evictions as warm KV caches missed.
- Symptoms: increased tail latency (p95 -> 2.8s from 180ms), token-level error 503 for ~2m at peak, partially filled token cache leading to cache-miss amplification.

Immediate reproduction steps I used (local emulation):
1) Replayed synthetic load using ab (quick) and wrk (sustained):
   wrk -t12 -c400 -d120s -s scripts/post.lua http://lb-hosted/v1/generate?model=redwood-medium
2) Simulated AZ capacity differences by tainting nodes in k8s control plane test cluster:
   kubectl label node ip-10-1-2-34 failure-sim=az-east-2-tainted --overwrite
3) Forced eviction logic path by setting lower threshold in the routing policy:
   PUT /admin/policy/zonal-eviction {"evict_threshold":0.65, "stabilization_window_sec":30}

Commands and key outputs I captured:
- List routes that were re-elected:
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://api.redwood.internal/admin/routes/recent?since=2026-03-08T17:30Z
   -> returns JSON list (trimmed): [
     {"route":"/v1/generate", "reasons": ["zonal-evict", "cache-miss-penalty"]},
     {"route":"/v1/embed", "reasons": ["none"]}
   ]
- Routing decision debug (per-request header trace):
   X-RW-Routing-Trace: chosen=az-west-1, fallback=az-east-2 (elected: az-west-1 priority 0.9), reason=evict(0.68 > 0.65)
- Example eviction log snippet from control-plane logs:
   2026-03-08T17:44:02Z [eviction-manager] route=/v1/generate zone=az-east-2 score=0.68 threshold=0.65 action=eject pods=[pod-aaaa,pod-bbbb]
- KV cache miss amplification metric (post-incident metric dump):
   kv_cache_fill_ratio{zone=az-east-2,route=/v1/generate}=0.24
   kv_cache_fill_ratio{zone=az-west-1,route=/v1/generate}=0.78
- Autoscaler churn: several scale-downs attempted while traffic was still spiky. Example HPA event:
   Normal  2026-03-08T17:45:00Z  monkey-hpa  ScalingReplicaSet  Scaled down replica set job-xxxxx to 2

Error snippets I saw in service logs (copied raw):
- "rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = connection closed"
- "route_eject: candidate zone az-east-2 score 0.68 < threshold 0.70 cause=eviction-policy"
- "cachealk: prefix-mismatch: expected token 0x3a4 got 0x1f2 — treating as miss"

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Thresholds tuned too aggressively for short spikes — current evict_threshold=0.70 with stabilization_window 15s is too small, causing premature ejections on transient QPS spikes.
2) Autoscaler and eviction manager race: HPA sees CPU/memory drop (because requests are failing fast) and scales down, further reducing capacity and making eviction decisions worse (positive feedback loop).
3) KV cache had a cold-start window after ejection; when combined with a model that has large KV footprint (chat history), cache refills were slow and cache-miss penalty increased effective load by 30–50%.
4) Per-route cost model underestimates worst-case sequence lengths under spike leading to overloaded pods even if nominal CPU metrics look fine.
5) Misattributed metric source: one of the telemetry collectors was reporting stale AZ-level free_gpus metric for az-east-2 (delayed ingestion ~20s), making the controller think there was less capacity than there actually was.

Quick checks I ran to test hypothesis 5:
- Checked telemetry lag:
   curl -sS https://telemetry.internal/metrics/last_ingest?zone=az-east-2&metric=free_gpus
   -> last_ingest=2026-03-08T17:43:25Z (which was ~37s before the eviction log at 17:44:02Z).
- Verified probe timeline (k8s node exporter):
   kubectl get events -n infra | grep 'node-exporter' | tail -n 10
   -> shows restart at 17:42:40Z on node ip-10-1-2-34 (coincides with spike)
Conclusion: possible telemetry lag + exporter restart made the controller conservative.

Mitigations applied (short-term):
- Raised evict_threshold to 0.75 for the problematic route group with immediate PUT to admin API to reduce ejections during stabilization.
- Increased stabilization_window_sec to 60s for all 'latency-sensitive' routes.
- Pinned dedicated KV-cache population job to run on scale-up events for the route (experiment) so warm cache stakes get a headstart.

Commands used to apply mitigations:
   curl -XPUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" -d '{"evict_threshold":0.75,"stabilization_window_sec":60}' https://api.redwood.internal/admin/policy/zonal-eviction

Notes about the playbook and changes to test:
- We should reproduce with synthetic telemetry lag to ensure the controller does not over-eject when telemetry is stale. Plan: run wrk + kill node-exporter process on one node to emulate restart, observe decision timeline.
- Add a canary config to run the new stabilization window only for a subset of traffic (10%) and monitor p95 / error rate for 30m before global rollout.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Is the eviction score calculation documented somewhere? I couldn't find a concise formula in code comments. Action: ping @Daniel to point me at the relevant function in the controller repo.
- Decide whether to add a telemetry_lag buffer to the eviction manager (e.g., ignore samples older than X seconds or weight them down).
- Should we make the autoscaler aware of eviction decisions? Possibly add an HPA annotation to prevent scale-down in the first N seconds after an eviction event.
- Run an offline sim with current eviction parameters and historical traffic from 2026-02-20 -> 2026-03-08 to estimate false positive ejection rate.

Notes to self (commands to re-run later):
- Recreate event: set evict_threshold to 0.65, stabilization_window to 15, run wrk for 90s with 500 concurrency and taint nodes in one AZ, capture logs:
   kubectl taint nodes --all simulate-evict=true:NoSchedule  (use test cluster)
   wrk -t12 -c500 -d90s -s scripts/post.lua http://lb-hosted/v1/generate?model=redwood-medium
   tail -f /var/log/infra/eviction-manager.log | sed -n '1,200p'

Slack breadcrumbs: thread-ids / quick refs:
- infra-ops thread CA12345 (incident notification)
- #serving-runtime channel: permalink to discussion about cache warming (p/CK9A2F)

Useful snippets to copy into a formal postmortem:
- "Telemetry lag + exporter restart + aggressive eviction threshold created a short positive feedback loop; mitigation: increase stabilization window and introduce telemetry freshness check."
- "Autoscaler and eviction manager need a coordinated signal; treat recent eviction events as 'no-scale-down' hints for N seconds."

Next steps (for me):
- Create small PR to add telemetry_lag_seconds sanity check in eviction manager (unit tests + docs).
- Add a dashboard panel that shows eviction events overlayed on telemetry ingestion times.
- Coordinate with SRE to run controlled chaos experiment (node-exporter restart + synthetic traffic) in the canary cluster.

References and artifacts (for follow-up):
- JIRA-INF-4982 (incident ticket)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2316 (candidate changes for stabilize window)
- Confluence draft: Zonal Eviction Playbook (link above)

Random thought I had while debugging:
- Could we use a tiny secondary probe that cross-checks GPU allocation directly (sidecar) instead of relying on node-exporter metrics aggregated through our standard pipeline? That would give ~2–3s fresher signal. Worth prototyping.

End of scratch notes — keep this informal. If this turns into a runbook I'll extract the commands and laminate a checklist for on-call.
